extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether a patent application's specification satisfies the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph — i.e., whether the specification shows the inventor was in possession of the claimed invention. The page gives principles, procedures, examples, and case law for examiners (and practitioners) to apply during prosecution and claim amendment review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description requirement — general principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification shall contain a written description of the invention (35 U.S.C. 112, para. 1). This requirement is separate and distinct from enablement and implements the principle that a patent must describe the technology sought to be patented; it serves to demonstrate that the inventor was in possession of the claimed subject matter and to put the public in possession of what is claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy objectives: convey that applicant invented the claimed subject matter and put the public in possession. Case law cited (e.g., Vas-Cath, Univ. of Rochester v. Searle, Capon v. Eshhar). Rejections are based on substantive law; Guidelines assist Office personnel but do not have force of law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession standard — must show applicant had possession of claimed invention
rubrics_metrics.description: To satisfy the written description requirement, the specification must describe the claimed invention in sufficient detail that one skilled in the art can reasonably conclude the inventor had possession of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possession may be shown by words, structures, figures, diagrams, formulas; description of reduction to practice or evidence that invention was 'ready for patenting' (drawings, structural chemical formulas), or by distinguishing identifying characteristics sufficient to show possession. Cite Lockwood, Pfaff, Eli Lilly, Amgen v. Chugai.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description is fact-based and varies with the nature of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Compliance is essentially a fact-based inquiry that will necessarily vary depending on the nature of the invention claimed and must be decided case-by-case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should consider the nature of the art and amount of knowledge imparted to those skilled in the art by the disclosure. Case law: Enzo Biochem, Vas-Cath, In re Wertheim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original claims presumption and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a strong presumption that an adequate written description of the claimed invention is present when the application is filed, but the presumption can fail if aspects of the claimed invention are not described with sufficient particularity (e.g., essential or critical features not disclosed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original-claim rejections should be rare; when an original claim requires an essential feature not described in spec and that feature is not conventional or known, the claim as a whole may not be adequately described (examples: gene claims where promoters, coding regions, regulatory elements may be implicitly included). Case citations: In re Wertheim, LizardTech, Eli Lilly, In re Bell/Deuel discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim-by-claim analysis and broadest reasonable interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Each claim must be separately analyzed and given its broadest reasonable interpretation in light of and consistent with the written description; the examiner must determine what the claim as a whole covers (including preamble and transitional phrase).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim construction is essential. Consider preamble language, transitional phrases ('comprising' = open-ended; 'consisting essentially of' = middle ground), and include weight given to preamble and transitional terms. See In re Morris, Genentech v. Chiron, PPG v. Guardian, Pac-Tec v. Amerace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate support for each element/limitation/step in claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Review the entire application to understand how the applicant provides support for the claimed invention, including each element and/or step; an applicant shows possession by describing the claimed invention with all of its limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine specification, claims, figures, examples, and incorporated material for support. Determine if sufficient structures, acts, or functions are recited to make clear the scope and meaning of the claim. Absence of definitions for well-established terms should not be the basis for rejection, but limitations may not be imported into claims from the specification. (See Lockwood, Bell Communications Research, Corning Glass Works.)

rubrics_metrics.name: New or amended claims must be supported by original disclosure (no new matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proscription against introduction of new matter prevents adding information beyond the originally filed subject matter; new or amended claims that introduce unsupported elements or limitations violate the written description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New limitations must be supported by express, implicit, or inherent disclosure in the original specification. Corrections of obvious errors may be permissible when one skilled in the art would recognize the error and appropriate correction (In re Oda). For sequence corrections and biological material, special rules apply (see 37 CFR 1.801 et seq., 1.804). See cases: In re Rasmussen, In re Lukach, In re Smith, Benno.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant must show support for amendments; examiner initial burden for rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: When claims are amended, applicant should specifically point out where the originally filed disclosure supports the amendments; the examiner has the initial burden of presenting evidence or reasoning why persons skilled in the art would not recognize support for the claim amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §§714.02, 2163.06, 2163.04. If applicant points out support and examiner finds disclosure does not reasonably convey possession, examiner must present reasoning. Rejection of original claims for lack of written description should be rare (Wertheim).

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of an element disclosed as essential can create written description problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Omitting a limitation that the specification describes as an essential or critical feature may indicate the inventor did not possess a broader claimed invention, leading to lack of written description for the broader claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: claims broadened by removing location or mixing elements where spec described a composition; if spec states a particular understanding is 'the only possible location' or essential, broader claim may be invalid for lack of written description. Cases: PIN/NIP v. Platte Chem., Gentry Gallery, Tronzo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional-only descriptions (especially biomolecules) are often insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: A biomolecule sequence described only by a functional characteristic, without a known or disclosed correlation between function and structure, normally is not a sufficient identifying characteristic for written description purposes, even when accompanied by a method of obtaining the claimed sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional language that does not identify structural characteristics generally fails for written description (In re Bell, In re Deuel). By contrast, software functions may suffice in some circumstances where code is within skill of the art (Fonar v. GE — flow charts/source code not always required).

rubrics_metrics.name: Process-disclosed products and foreseeability to skilled artisan
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure of a process may not adequately describe the product unless the knowledge and level of skill in the art would permit one skilled in the art to immediately envisage the product claimed from the disclosed process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Laundry list' disclosures of many possible moieties do not describe every species in a genus if they would not reasonably lead skilled artisans to any particular species (Fujikawa, In re Ruschig). Examiners should assess whether the disclosure would reasonably lead to the claimed species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherency as support — standards and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosing a device that inherently performs a function or has a property means the application discloses that function/theory/advantage even if not explicitly stated, and the application may later be amended to recite it without new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To establish inherency the evidence must make clear the missing descriptive matter is necessarily present and recognized by persons of ordinary skill; inherency cannot be established by probabilities or possibilities. Case law: In re Reynolds, In re Smythe, In re Robertson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporation by reference treated as part of original application
rubrics_metrics.description: Material properly incorporated by reference into the specification is treated as part of the application as filed; replacing incorporated material with the actual text is not new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow 37 CFR 1.57 and MPEP §608.01(p) regarding incorporation by reference. Consider impact when analyzing 35 U.S.C. 112 second paragraph or sixth paragraph issues (see MPEP §2181).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deposits of biological materials — limited role and requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A deposit made in accordance with 37 CFR 1.801 et seq. may satisfy the written description requirement for claimed biological materials but is not a substitute for a written description; the written description of deposited material needs to be as complete as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deposits provide antecedent basis and aid verification but examination proceeds solely on the written description. Deposits made after filing cannot support additions or corrections to the original disclosure unless specific regulatory statements are filed (see 37 CFR 1.804). See Final Rule and In re Lundak guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: No in haec verba requirement; support may be express, implicit, or inherent
rubrics_metrics.description: While literal wording is not required ('in haec verba' is not required), claim limitations added later must have support in the specification by express, implicit, or inherent disclosure and cannot introduce new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples where genus/species interplay matters: a subgenus is not necessarily described by a genus plus an example species. Case law: In re Lukach, In re Smith. Corrections of obvious errors are allowed when recognizable by a skilled artisan (In re Oda).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rephrasing and dictionary/art-recognized definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere rephrasing of a passage that keeps the same meaning does not constitute new matter; inclusion of dictionary or art-recognized definitions known at filing time is generally permissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If multiple definitions exist and a definition is added later, it must be clear from original application that applicant intended that particular definition to avoid new matter/lack of written description (Scarring Corp. v. Megan example renaming 'leukocyte interferon' to 'IFN-(a)').

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction of sequencing errors and post-filing deposits — constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Corrections of minor sequencing errors may be possible if a skilled artisan would resequence and immediately recognize the error; deposits made after filing generally cannot be relied upon to support corrections unless applicant complies with regulatory statements (37 CFR 1.804).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequencing errors are common; when sequence info references a deposit made in accordance with regulations, special considerations apply. See discussion of Peter Richterich and In re Oda-type corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim language and transitional phrase impact on scope and written description analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Transitional phrases ('comprising', 'consisting essentially of', 'consisting of') and preamble language affect claim scope and thus what must be supported in the specification; absent clear indication of basic and novel characteristics, 'consisting essentially of' may be construed as 'comprising' for prior art purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants bear burden to show that additional steps/materials would materially change invention when relying on 'consisting essentially of' language. Case citations: PPG v. Guardian, AK Steel, In re De Lajarte, Ex parte Davis.
